children.name: Teacher Planning, Grading, and Feedback
children.blurb: Fifteen teachers in five primary schools in England used AI to help plan lessons for two school terms. Their self reported weekly planning time fell by 52.5 percent, from about 10 hours to under 5 (Carson et al., 2026).

children.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System
children.blurb: Researchers who build systems to predict student failure found something troubling when they looked closely. A single accuracy number made predictions look more reliable than they were.

children.name: Operations, Facilities, Transportation, and Finance
children.blurb: Boston Public Schools once faced a transportation problem that cost more than $100 million a year. Researchers built an optimization system that redesigned the bus routes, saving about $5 million a year and removing 50 buses while keeping service quality (Bertsimas et al., 2019).

children.name: People, Leadership, and Culture
children.blurb: Researchers interviewed leaders in six Colorado school districts about how they first responded to AI. Some wrote informal guidelines, some banned student use, and some updated their acceptable use policies (McGuire et al., 2026).

sections.body: This part of the book turns to the daily work of running a school and a district, covering teacher planning and grading, assessment and data, operations and finance, and people and leadership. It speaks most directly to principals, district leaders, and board members, since these are the roles that carry the work described. AI here is not treated as a separate subject but as something woven into the tasks these leaders already manage. The final chapter states the core argument of the Volume in full and sets out a plan for the first 90 days, and a short conclusion looks back at what the evidence shows and ahead to what may change.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book holds that these chapters speak most directly to principals, district leaders, and board members, which is where it places its confidence about who can act on the material. It does not claim that every part of running a school changes at once, and it keeps the final chapter focused on stating the core argument in full rather than adding new claims. What works, as the book frames it, is a plan for the first 90 days that follows from that argument, and what does not work is treating the argument as something to admire without a plan attached. The rule it holds to is that the evidence should be looked at honestly, both for what it shows now and for what may change later.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages fit together as the working sequence of running a school, and each one answers a different question a leader or teacher would bring. Teacher Planning, Grading, and Feedback is where a teacher or principal goes for the instructional work that sits closest to students, while Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System is where a leader goes to understand how data is used to notice problems early. Operations, Facilities, Transportation, and Finance is the page for the practical and financial side that keeps a school running, and People, Leadership, and Culture is where a principal, district leader or board member goes for the human side of the work. A parent would find the first of these most familiar, since it touches grading and feedback, and the rest explain the systems behind the school their child attends.
